To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
there is a correlation between the latency differences of neighbouring ganglion cells and the lags of their maintained discharge, but that there are often large differences between the two.

(1) the differences between the latencies of pairs of ganglion cells are generally twice the magnitude of the lags of their maintained discharge, (2) the differences in the times to the response peaks of pairs of ganglia cells are generally greater than the magnitude of the cross‐correlation lags, and (3) there is a strong negative correlation between latency (or lag) and the rise time of the response.

the lags of pairs of retinal ganglions cells are strongly correlated with the difference in latency of the responses to a light stimulus, that the lags are not correlated with the difference between the magnitudes (or the rise times) of the responses, that the relationship between latency difference and lags does not depend on whether the members of pairs are X‐like or non‐X‐like cells and that there is a correlation between maintained discharge rates and latencies.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between the latency of the response of a retinal ganglion cell to a light stimulus and its maintained discharge rate.
the relationship between the response latencies of pairs of neurones and the time‐lag in the maintained activity of the same cells.
a study of the temporal characteristics of the responses of pairs of retinal neurones in the isolated gold‐fish retina.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the lags between the maintained discharge of pairs of ganglion cells are correlated with differences in latency of response to flashes of light.

the lags of pairs of ganglion cells correlate strongly with the differences in the latency of the responses to repeated stimuli, but not with the differences in time to the peak of the responses, nor with the differences in magnitude of the responses.
there is a relationship between the differences in latency of the responses of two units and the lags of their maintained discharges, but the relationship is not as simple as one might wish.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

(1) the latency of the response to a flash is related to the maintained rate; (2) differences in latency are related to differences in lag; (3) the latency of a cell is related to the latency of its neighbours; and (4) the latency of an individual cell is related to its response magnitude.

there are at least three factors which contribute to the differences in response latency of neighbouring ganglion cells: (1) the maintained discharge rate of a neurones; (2) the rise time of the response; (3) the differential conduction velocity of axons.
the lags of pairs of cells are related to differences in latency but not to differences in time‐ to‐peak, magnitude, or response categorizations.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the differences in the latencies of pairs of ganglion cells in goldfish retina are greater than their lags and that these differences are related to the maintained rates of the cells and their rise times.
there are two different ways to measure the time‐course of the response of a neurone to light, the latency and lag measures.
the latency difference between two units is a good indicator of the lag between them.
